title: Learning trumpet, Willie Foster's band and the Pelican band
summary: His father's spasm band, buying a cornet, correspondence course and lessons, joining Willie Foster, then the Pelican band with its coaching, new arrangements and raided personnel.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Well I was born August 10th, 1905 and all around the house there, you know I always had inspiration to play music. My daddy tried to get me to play drums. You know I always talked to him about a set of drums. Because they needed a drummer in their band, you see they had, they called that band a spasm band. They had three-piece. They had a violin, guitar, and string bass. And so one day my brother saw a cornet, one of the short brass cornet. He bought the cornet for twelve dollars. So he came around the house, he never could play anything on them. So my daddy was still trying to get me to play drums, see. I said I picked up the trumpet, this cornet one day, an old man, they call him Manny Gabriel, he's an old musician, you know. He's a trumpet player. And the boat used to come over the lake there, it started a camellia. He made a red of it, on the river there, a camellia. Well they used to come over on Sundays and there's a tune I loved to hear him play. And that was, what's the name of the tune again? I can't think of. Pomet. Thailand stuff you know, but everyone knew what I was trying to play. So there's another fellow called Black Eagle, he and I started out together, so first little job we played some people, white people hired us to play for a party. We two went back then to play for the party, first little job we played. And I came on back and he never did decide to read Miss or to read Miss, so I came on back and I got out of that one and learned how to read Miss. So the first lesson I took was Mr. Parrish, he's an old Mortimer, I call his white fellow, he looks the scales out, the scales out for me. The first lesson I took was from him. So I decided when I came to New Orleans in 1919, I was in the American School of Music, you know, home and coast, so I decided to send him off for this home and coast. So I sent off for it, that was in around 1922 I think that it was, before that, but anyway during the time I was in front. So when I sent for this course I had took about, I guess about 14, 12, 14 lessons. And Willie Forster, Pop Forster's brother, you know, Pop Forster's brother, heard about me up there, he was up living uptown playing trumpet. So he came to my house and asked me about playing, see. So I told him, I said, well I'm not good enough to play yet, I said, but I'm going to go take a few lessons, I went to pitch back. Tiro, he was the head of the PWA band, you know, the head and you know. So after I went by him to take lessons, he asked me, say, boy who's been teaching you? I said, no one. I said, I've been taking correspondence. He said, well I'll be doggone, people tell me you can't learn that way. He said, well you better know some scholars I've been teaching two years. I said, you can read better some scholars I've been teaching two years. Well I inspired you, I gave you inspiration to go on, you know. So I came back and told Willie Forster, yes I can play in your band. So he got his band, I tell you, me playing trumpet, Bigger Ennis Keller, Leda Ennis Keller. He had Albert Fader, I don't know if he's living still, but Crump, Lil Crump, Leda Trump, he's playing saxophone. We had the Sun Johnson, you all know him, I know. I've never heard of him, I know, Sun Johnson, his name is Augustine Johnson, we all call him Sun. A lot of the fellas call him Bobo, you know. So we got him, the four of us, Willie Forster, and his son-in-law rather, and we started playing out there, bunk up to the space, every Friday, Saturday night, that's below the, on the other side of the levee, you know. We played out there. And through playing with him, Frank Jarrett heard about me on the Pelican. He needed a trumpet player. So he came up, called him and got, and I said, man we need a trumpet player. So I went on the Pelican, started playing with the Pelican. Well that's where the name, the Pelican Silverstone was, and I still use it, you know. I use it, the Black Pelicans, that's where I use it now. We started on the Pelican. Well I played on the Pelican about, let's see, now I'm sure, it must have been about three years. About three years, yeah. Well after we got the band there on the Pelican, the band was so good in reading music and playing music, until Miss Amber Lily Mae Hubbard, she used to come in singing the band and kind of coach the band, you know. She was a member of the Green Pastures. She was singing in Green Pastures. Now she used to go to New York and buy anything. She'd buy overtures for us to play with a ten piece band, see. She just thought we could play anything. I'll tell you, one number she bought for us, Headlow, that's one of the numbers she bought for us, and it brought another one, Listernia, that was another one. We played that. We also played Louisiana Bobo, we were the first band down there to play Louisiana Bobo. So the band got good and you know how the older fellas are, when they see young men coming up and they're good, they come pick out just who they want out of the band, see. The main others, they just try to tear the band down and keep them doing them some more, you know. I found out later, you know, later, but I didn't know the other thing. So first man that come and got out of the band, Alvin Alcorn was playing second trumpet with me, man. Alvin Alcorn, they took Alvin Alcorn out of the band, Don Amber did that, took Alvin Alcorn out of the band. No, it wasn't, no it wasn't, Alvin Alcorn, had a professor, he taught at school at, Professor Dedeson, he taught at school at New Orleans University at that time, New Orleans I think it's Dillard now. He took Alvin Alcorn, Frank Jackhead, which was the leader of the band, you know, he was the leader of the trombone player there. And he took Jim, the bass tuba player, the human bass tuba there. He took our bass tuba player, I can't think of his name, it was the name of the band, and how he took the three men out. Well that led me to have to get, replace three men, see. I replaced Alvin Alcorn with Leo Dejong. And I replaced Frank with, what's this old man, Sonny Henry, Sonny Henry. Sonny Henry and I replaced the bass play with Boise Gregg, his name, you know. He was an old show man. He was a great trumpet player also, you know, played bass too. But he replaced them. Well about time the band got pretty good, well they took some other men out of the band, see them? They took Sonny Johnson out of the band. Sonny Johnson, that's who else they took. I remember Sonny, the one, he was playing first sax. And, oh yeah, the piano player had left that time, so we got Emily Hyman was playing with, late Emily Hyman, she was playing with us during that time. We got Camilla Todd, you know Camilla Todd is Clarence Todd's brother, our sister brother, you know. And Clarence Todd. You remember Clarence Todd from, he's in Chicago, he's a piano player, he's arranging, we call him steeplehead, he's got a head like a steeplehead.
